abstract.p: The Alia musica was not conceived by a single author at a single time. Instead, it is the result of a layering of commentaries by successive authors (β, γ and δ) upon a core treatise (Author α). The text-historical edition represents this process of commenting in its chronological order, as outlined by Charles M. Atkinson, The Critical Nexus: Tone-System, Mode, and Notation in Early Medieval Music (Oxford, New York: Oxford University Press, 2009): 171-201. This edition does not represent a specific manuscript or an archetype of transmission, but is intended to display the stages of commentary in chronological order. Each stage in the genesis of the text can be accessed separately.

Author δ played a particularly important role in the creation of the final text. He acted not only as a commentator, but also structured the treatise as we know it from the manuscript transmission by adding headings and changing the order of the material, placing most of the core treatise, α, at the end of the work. A comparison between the genealogical order of commenting and the final arrangement, as represented in the manuscripts, is provided by the overview.
This is the core treatise for the Alia musica, Atkinson’s Author α, dating from the late 9th century. It presents 8 toni, or church modes, describing each both verbally and mathematically.
This presents the core treatise by Author α as framed and commented upon by a second author, Atkinson´s Author β (early 10th c.).

This presents the core treatise (Author α), its frame and commentary (Author β), and a tonary, the Nova expositio (Author γ), transmitted independently, but added to the first two layers (later 10th c.).

This presents the sum of the core treatise and its commentaries. All parts of the text are located in the order by which the commentary grew before Author δ’s final redaction, which shifted Author α’s work to the end of the treatise, where we find it in the manuscripts of the complete work.

This presents the organization of the entire treatise before and after Author δ’s rearrangement of the order of materials. „α + β + γ + δ“ shows the sum of the core treatise and its commentaries, „Manuscript Order“ shows the arrangement of the text as we find it in the manuscripts (e.g. Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, clm 14272, and Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, lat. 7211) – the arrangement that Author δ created when he shifted from commenting to redacting the final version of the treatise.
